title: Λύκος καὶ γραῦς
titleEn: The Wolf and the Old Woman
part: The Wolf and the Old Woman (Chambry 223)
source: Émile Chambry, Ésope: Fables, texte établi et traduit (Les Belles Lettres, Paris, 1927), fable 223. Text as printed, including Chambry's editorial punctuation (« »). Pronunciation: reconstructed Attic, after W. S. Allen, Vox Graeca. Romanization: standard classical transliteration (ē/ō; th/ph/ch; y for υ, u in diphthongs; h = rough breathing; ēi/āi/ōi for iota subscript; accents omitted).

sentences.l: A wolf, being famished, was going about seeking food.
sentences.n: περιῄει is the imperfect of περίειμι, 'go round', and two participles hang from it — λιμώττων giving his condition, ζητῶν his errand. This double-participle opening is the standard first move of a fable.

sentences.t: Γενόμενος δὲ κατά τινα τόπον, ἤκουσε παιδίου κλαίοντος καὶ γραὸς λεγούσης αὐτῷ· « Παῦσαι τοῦ κλαίειν· εἰ δὲ μή, τῇ ὥρᾳ ταύτῃ ἐπιδώσω σε τῷ λύκῳ. »
sentences.tr: Genomenos de kata tina topon, ēkouse paidiou klaiontos kai graos legousēs autōi· « Pausai tou klaiein· ei de mē, tēi hōrāi tautēi epidōsō se tōi lykōi. »
sentences.l: And having come to a certain place, he heard a small child crying and an old woman saying to it: « Stop your crying; and if not, at this very hour I shall give you over to the wolf. »
sentences.i: Coming to a certain place, he heard a small child crying and an old woman saying to it: « Stop that crying, or this very hour I shall hand you over to the wolf. »
sentences.n: ἀκούω takes the genitive of the person heard, with a supplementary participle for what they are doing: παιδίου κλαίοντος, a child in the act of crying. Παῦσαι is the aorist middle imperative, 'make yourself stop', with the articular infinitive τοῦ κλαίειν after it. εἰ δὲ μή, literally 'but if not', is Greek's standing 'otherwise', and it follows a command as readily as a statement.

sentences.t: Οἰόμενος δὲ ὁ λύκος ὅτι ἀληθεύει ἡ γραῦς, ἵστατο πολλὴν ἐκδεχόμενος ὥραν.
sentences.tr: Oiomenos de ho lykos hoti alētheuei hē graus, histato pollēn ekdechomenos hōran.
sentences.l: And the wolf, supposing that the old woman spoke truly, took his stand, waiting a long while.
sentences.i: The wolf supposed the old woman meant what she said, and stood there waiting a long while.
sentences.n: ὅτι after οἰόμενος keeps the present tense of the thought as it was thought, ἀληθεύει, where English shifts it back. ἵστατο is imperfect middle, of taking a position and holding it. ὥρα here is a stretch of time, not a reading of the clock.

sentences.t: Ὡς δ’ ἑσπέρα κατέλαβεν, ἀκούει πάλιν τῆς γραὸς κολακευούσης τὸ παιδίον καὶ λεγούσης αὐτῷ· « Ἐὰν ἔλθῃ ὁ λύκος δεῦρο, φονεύσομεν, ὦ τέκνον, αὐτόν. »
sentences.tr: Hōs d’ hespera katelaben, akouei palin tēs graos kolakeuousēs to paidion kai legousēs autōi· « Ean elthēi ho lykos deuro, phoneusomen, ō teknon, auton. »
sentences.l: And when evening came on, he hears again the old woman coaxing the child and saying to it: « If the wolf comes here, we shall kill him, my child. »
sentences.i: When evening had come on, he heard the old woman again, this time coaxing the child and saying to it: « If the wolf comes here, my child, we shall kill him. »
sentences.n: ἀκούει is a historic present dropped into past narrative for vividness; Greek does this freely and English will not usually carry it. καταλαμβάνω is used of the time of day overtaking a person. ἐάν with the aorist subjunctive is the vivid future condition. The vocative ὦ τέκνον sits inside its clause rather than at the head, as Greek prefers.

sentences.t: Ταῦτα ἀκούσας ὁ λύκος ἐπορεύετο λέγων· « Ἐν ταύτῃ τῇ ἐπαύλει ἄλλα μὲν λέγουσιν, ἄλλα δὲ πράττουσιν. »
sentences.tr: Tauta akousas ho lykos eporeueto legōn· « En tautēi tēi epaulei alla men legousin, alla de prattousin. »
sentences.l: Having heard these things, the wolf went on his way saying: « In this steading they say one thing and do another. »
sentences.n: ἄλλα μέν … ἄλλα δέ, 'some things … other things', is the regular Greek for 'one thing … another'. ἔπαυλις is the whole farmstead, fold and house together. ἐπορεύετο is imperfect: he was already on his way as he said it.

sentences.t: Ὁ μῦθος πρὸς ἀνθρώπους οἵτινες τὰ ἔργα τοῖς λόγοις οὐκ ἔχουσιν ὅμοια.
sentences.tr: Ho mythos pros anthrōpous hoitines ta erga tois logois ouk echousin homoia.
sentences.l: The fable is directed at people who do not have their deeds like their words.
sentences.i: The fable is directed at people whose deeds do not match their words.
sentences.n: ὅμοιος takes the dative of what a thing resembles, τοῖς λόγοις. οἵτινες is the generalising relative — not these particular people but anyone of the kind. The main clause has no verb at all: πρός with the accusative carries it, as it does in the other closing formulas of this shape.
